node-1.label: Infant presented with nystagmus and right exotropia

node-2.label: No family history of retinoblastoma; known untreated atrial septal defect

node-3.label: Fundus examination revealed bilateral involvement, with a tumor in the right eye and an isolated anterior tumor in the left eye

node-4.label: Neurological examination initially normal at baseline; two days after procedure, patient presented with status epilepticus and left upper extremity weakness; follow-up at 6 months showed full strength in the upper and lower extremities and normal tone

why.why: Bilateral retinal tumors on fundus examination strongly support bilateral retinoblastoma as the cause of nystagmus and right exotropia. No family history favors a non-familial presentation. Brain MRI shows a right MCA territory infarct with absent A1 segment, which explains the transient post-procedure seizures and weakness as vascular and not a primary neurological disorder, thereby removing a competing explanation for the ocular findings. Echocardiography confirmed a moderate left-to-right shunt without thrombus or vegetation, consistent with the known ASD and not refuting the ocular diagnosis. RB1 germline testing and orbital MRI remain unavailable, so heritable risk and extraocular extension cannot be fully excluded, but these gaps do not change the primary diagnosis of bilateral retinoblastoma. Confidence is increased from 0.82 to 0.9.

The initial normal neurological baseline and full recovery from transient post-procedure seizures and weakness already made a primary neurological disorder unlikely. Brain MRI now demonstrates a right MCA territory infarct with absent A1 segment, providing a clear vascular explanation for these transient symptoms. This new imaging evidence further refutes a primary neurological disorder as the cause of the ocular signs, reducing confidence from 0.12 to 0.04.

Untreated atrial septal defect and bilateral retinal tumors raise the possibility of a congenital/genetic syndrome, but no additional syndromic features are present. Echocardiography confirmed a moderate left-to-right shunt without thrombus or vegetation, consistent with an isolated ASD. RB1 germline testing and orbital MRI remain unavailable, so a heritable germline mutation cannot be fully excluded; however, the overall picture remains most consistent with bilateral retinoblastoma as the primary diagnosis, and a broader congenital/genetic syndrome is less likely. Confidence is slightly reduced from 0.06 to 0.05.
